implementation_notes: Boost.Lockfree ships the whole structure: boost::lockfree::queue is the Michael-Scott MPMC queue, bounded_ticket_queue the Vyukov bounded variant, and spsc_queue a wait-free single-producer/single-consumer ringbuffer; the library's own documentation warns that node-pool exhaustion falls back to the OS allocator (blocking, unless fixed_sized/capacity is configured) and that the lock-free guarantee bounds operation cost only in the worst case, so benchmark against a mutex first. Use it as the default. The hand-rolled std::atomic realization is the fallback when Boost cannot be linked and the reclamation scheme can be owned, and folly::MPMCQueue when the codebase is already on folly and a bounded, futex-blocking ticket ring fits.
pitfalls: boost::lockfree::queue allocates nodes from a pool; when it is exhausted it calls the OS allocator, which is not lock-free - configure capacity<>/fixed_sized for real-time use.
Boost.Lockfree deliberately avoids exceptions in lock-free code; a throwing payload constructor or allocator breaks the real-time claim.
The hand-rolled variants still need a reclamation scheme: C++26 brings std::hazard_pointer, before it epochs or a type-stable pool must be owned.

variants.name: Hand-rolled Michael-Scott queue over std::atomic
variants.implementation_notes: std::atomic<Node*> with compare_exchange_weak is enough for the link and endpoint swaps, but not for freeing: before C++26's std::hazard_pointer the queue must ship its own epoch or hazard reclamation (or use a type-stable pool), and the memory orders - release on publication, acquire on the claim - carry the correctness. Choose this only when Boost or folly cannot be added, or when the structure must be tuned to a specific workload; reproduce the published pseudocode rather than improvising the tail-advance step.
pitfalls: Getting the tail-advance step wrong leaves the queue correct but progressively slower as the tail lags behind.
Without epochs or hazard pointers the first concurrent dequeue is a use-after-free; there is no standard reclamation before C++26.

variants.name: folly::MPMCQueue bounded ticket ring
variants.idiom_name: folly::MPMCQueue<T> (ticket dispenser + per-slot CAS + futex blocking)
variants.implementation_notes: folly::MPMCQueue is a fixed-capacity ring whose head and tail are ticket dispensers (atomic increment, more robust under contention than a CAS loop) and whose slots each own a single-element queue with an adaptive spin then futex block; the header documents linearizability and requires T to be nothrow-move-constructible. Capacity is fixed and every byte is allocated up front, so it is the allocation-free choice - at the price of a folly dependency (C++17 toolchain) and a hard bound: write() returns false when full, so a backpressure policy must exist above it.
pitfalls: Capacity is a hard limit and write() fails rather than growing, so backpressure policy is mandatory.
The queue statically requires nothrow-move-constructible payloads; a throwing move is a compile error, not a runtime surprise.
